seoTitle: Michigan Shoulder Dystocia Lawyer – Was the Delivery Handled Properly?
seoDescription: Shoulder dystocia in a Michigan delivery: the maneuver sequence, the two things a physician must never do, how long is too long, the injuries to baby and mother, and what the delivery note must show. Deadlines and 2026 caps. Free review.
tagline: Shoulder dystocia cannot be predicted. How it is handled can be judged, minute by minute, from the delivery note.

c.v: Shoulder dystocia is the obstetric emergency that happens after the baby’s head is born: the front shoulder lodges behind the mother’s pubic bone and the body does not follow. The umbilical cord is compressed in the birth canal, the baby cannot breathe, and the physician has a few minutes to free the shoulder using a trained sequence of maneuvers. Done correctly, most shoulder dystocias end with a healthy baby. Done incorrectly, or too slowly, they end with a torn brachial plexus, a fractured collarbone or arm, a brain injured by lack of oxygen, or a baby who does not survive, and often with serious injury to the mother.

The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists puts the incidence at 0.2 to 3 percent of vaginal deliveries. Michigan recorded 99,420 births in 2024, about two-thirds of them vaginal, which means somewhere between a few hundred and roughly two thousand Michigan deliveries a year involve a shoulder dystocia. Most are resolved in under a minute by McRoberts positioning and suprapubic pressure and leave no trace but a line in the delivery note.

What distinguishes a shoulder dystocia case from a shoulder dystocia is what the physician and nurses did when the shoulder stuck. ACOG says plainly that shoulder dystocia cannot be reliably predicted or prevented, and defense lawyers quote that sentence in every case. It is true, and it is beside the point. The standard of care is not that the shoulder never sticks; it is that when it does, the team recognizes it, calls for help, works through the maneuvers in sequence, never pushes on the top of the uterus, never pulls hard on the baby’s head, and documents what it did and when. Every one of those steps leaves a record. This page explains what the standard required, the injuries to the baby and to the mother, how a Michigan case is proved and defended, the damages and 2026 caps, and the deadlines.

What the standard requires is that appropriate maneuvers be used promptly, with the team moving to another maneuver when one is unsuccessful.

sections.heading: The two things that must never be done

c.v: The maneuvers are what the standard requires. Two actions are what it prohibits, and they are at the center of most shoulder dystocia lawsuits.

Pushing down on the top of the uterus drives the impacted shoulder harder against the pubic bone, increases the force on the brachial plexus, and can rupture the uterus. ACOG states it should not be used. It still happens, usually by a nurse acting on instinct or on a physician’s instruction, and it is frequently the mother or a family member who remembers it, because it is rarely charted.

Pulling the baby’s head downward and sideways to free the shoulder stretches the nerves of the brachial plexus on the side of the front shoulder. ACOG’s guidance is that the physician should avoid excessive lateral traction and should use the maneuvers instead of force. The 2014 ACOG task force report acknowledges that the forces of labor themselves can stretch the plexus, and hospitals rely on that finding in every case; the same report says the injury results from excess force, and a severe, permanent injury in a large baby after a long, documented dystocia is a pattern the records have to explain. While the shoulder is stuck, the cord is compressed and the baby is not getting oxygen. The baby’s blood becomes more acidic with each minute. Published studies have found that the risk of brain injury rises as the head-to-body interval lengthens, with permanent injury and death becoming substantially more likely beyond about five minutes, although a healthy baby at term can often tolerate a somewhat longer interval. ACOG does not set a hard limit; the standard is that the team move through the maneuvers without delay and that the interval be documented.

Two numbers in the delivery note therefore matter more than any other: the time the head delivered and the time the body delivered. A delivery note that omits them, or records a two-minute interval in a baby born with a pH of 6.9 and seizures, is itself evidence.

sections.heading: Proving a Michigan shoulder dystocia case

c.v: Michigan requires proof of the standard of care, breach, causation more probable than not, and damages, MCL 600.2912a, through experts who practice the same specialty as the defendant, MCL 600.2169. In a shoulder dystocia case the records and the experts line up as follows.

items.v: The prenatal record: estimated fetal weights and ultrasounds, glucose testing, the mother’s weight gain, any prior shoulder dystocia, and whether a delivery-planning discussion was documented.
The labor record and the electronic fetal monitoring archive, which shows the length of the second stage and whether vacuum or forceps were used.

, which ACOG says should document the time of delivery of the head and body, the maneuvers used and their sequence, which shoulder was anterior, who was present, the traction applied, the infant’s condition and cord gases, and the explanation given to the parents. A note that reads “shoulder dystocia, relieved with McRoberts and suprapubic pressure, infant to NICU” after a permanent injury is as telling as a detailed one.
The nursing notes, which often record what the physician’s note omits, including fundal pressure, who was called and when, and the times.
The newborn record: Apgar scores, cord gases, resuscitation, X-rays, the neurological exam, and NICU course.
The hospital’s shoulder dystocia protocol and its simulation training records, subject to any applicable peer-review privilege.

The question is how it was handled: whether the known risks were acted on before labor, whether the maneuvers were performed promptly and in sequence, whether fundal pressure or excessive traction was used, and how long the baby was without oxygen.

faqs.question: The doctor said the baby was big and that this just happens. Is that the end of it?

answer.v: No. If the baby was estimated at 5,000 grams or more, or 4,500 grams with diabetes, ACOG says a cesarean should have been offered, and the prenatal record shows whether that conversation happened. If the estimates were lower, the case turns on the management of the dystocia itself.

faqs.question: My baby’s arm was limp at birth. Is that always a permanent injury?

answer.v: No. Most brachial plexus injuries from shoulder dystocia are stretch injuries that recover within three months. About 15 percent persist beyond a year. A child with no biceps recovery by three months should be evaluated at a pediatric brachial plexus center.

faqs.question: The nurse pushed on my stomach. Was that wrong?

answer.v: Fundal pressure is prohibited in shoulder dystocia because it drives the shoulder harder into the bone and increases the force on the nerves. Suprapubic pressure, which is pressure just above the pubic bone, is a correct maneuver. Where the pressure was applied matters, and your account of it may be the only record.

There is no fixed limit, but the risk of brain injury rises as the head-to-body interval lengthens, and permanent injury becomes substantially more likely beyond about five minutes. The delivery note should record both times. If it does not, that omission is itself significant.

faqs.question: My baby was fine but I hemorrhaged and needed a hysterectomy. Do I have a claim?

answer.v: Possibly. Hemorrhage is the most common maternal complication of shoulder dystocia, and its management has a standard of care. A hysterectomy that resulted from mismanaged hemorrhage is the mother’s own malpractice claim, with a two-year deadline, and the loss of the ability to have children places it under Michigan’s higher cap.

faqs.question: Can we see the hospital’s training records?

answer.v: Michigan hospitals are expected to train for shoulder dystocia, and many run drills. Whether protocols and training records are discoverable depends on the hospital’s privilege claims, which the attorney will address.
